review.name: ACAS early conciliation
review.graph: Must have an employment dispute such as unfair dismissal, discrimination, unpaid wages or unlawful deduction.
review.note: The text limits early conciliation to people considering an employment tribunal claim, and elsewhere calls this a dispute with an employer, but it never names unfair dismissal, discrimination, unpaid wages or unlawful deduction as examples.
review.quote: Early conciliation is only for people who are considering making a claim to an employment tribunal.

review.name: Close a limited company
review.graph: Must be a director of a UK limited company that has not traded or otherwise been used for a purpose in the past 3 months.
review.note: The text says directors (with shareholders) are involved in closing a limited company, but it never mentions a condition that the company must not have traded or been used for any purpose in the past 3 months.
review.quote: You usually need to have the agreement of your company’s directors and shareholders to close a limited company.

review.name: File a confirmation statement
review.graph: Must be a registered company, LLP or eligible UK business entity.
review.note: The text implies the filer is a company registered with Companies House, but it never mentions LLPs or other eligible UK business entities.
review.quote: Include a cheque with your company number written on the back.

review.name: File annual accounts at Companies House
review.graph: Must be an officer of a UK limited company (Ltd or PLC).
review.note: The text says the service is for filing a company's accounts, but it never says the user must be an officer or that the company must be a Ltd or PLC, and it says LLPs can also use the service for certain package accounts.
review.quote: Use this service to file your company’s annual accounts with Companies House. Limited liability partnerships can only file certain package accounts using this service.

review.name: Register limited company (IN01)
review.graph: Registered office must be in England, Wales, Scotland, or Northern Ireland. No nationality restriction on directors or shareholders.
review.note: The text requires a UK registered office and says directors need not live in the UK, but it says nothing about nationality restrictions on directors or shareholders.
review.quote: Directors do not have to live in the UK but companies must have a UK registered office address.

review.name: Apply for teacher training
review.graph: Must have, or be working towards, a UK undergraduate degree (2:2 or above).
review.note: The text requires a degree or equivalent for postgraduate training, but it gives no 2:2 minimum, does not mention working towards a degree and does not require the degree to be from the UK.
review.quote: You need the following or equivalents: a degree

review.name: Care to Learn
review.graph: Parent must be under 20 at the start of the academic year.
review.note: The text gives the same under-20 age limit but measures it at the start of the course, not the start of the academic year.
review.quote: you’re a parent under 20 at the start of your course

review.name: National Careers Service
review.graph: Free adviser-led guidance is available to adults in England. Scotland, Wales and NI have their own careers services.
review.note: The text confirms you can get guidance from a careers adviser, but it does not say the service is free, for adults, or limited to England, and it does not mention separate services in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.
review.quote: Wherever you are with your decisions, you can contact us to get advice from a careers adviser.

review.name: Cancel driving licence
review.graph: Person with a GB driving licence has died.
review.note: The text covers telling DVLA that a driver with a licence has died, but it never says the licence must be a GB licence; it only says Northern Ireland has a different process.
review.quote: Write to DVLA to tell them a driver has died. Include the person’s driving licence with your letter, if you have it.

review.name: View and share driving licence
review.graph: Must hold a UK driving licence.
review.note: The text requires a licence issued in England, Wales or Scotland, which is narrower than 'UK driving licence' because it leaves out Northern Ireland licences (these get a separate link).
review.quote: You can view or share your driving licence information if your licence was issued in England, Wales or Scotland.

review.name: Update driving licence (name change)
review.graph: Has legally changed name following marriage, civil partnership, deed poll or court order.
review.note: The text covers changing your name and says original documents confirming the new name must be sent, but it never names marriage, civil partnership, deed poll or court order as routes, and never says the change must be legal.
review.quote: any original documents that confirm your new name or gender

review.name: Notify DVLA of medical condition
review.graph: Has a medical condition listed on DVLA's notifiable conditions list — including epilepsy, insulin-treated diabetes, visual impairment, sleep disorders, heart conditions, dementia, and many others.
review.note: The text says some medical conditions must be reported and gives an A to Z list that includes epilepsy, diabetes, eye conditions, sleep apnoea, heart conditions and dementia, but it never says 'insulin-treated' diabetes, and the list is framed as 'check if you need to report', not as a list of conditions that must be reported.
review.quote: You need to tell DVLA about some medical conditions as they can affect your driving.

review.name: Provisional Driving Licence
review.graph: Must be at least 15 years and 9 months old to apply. Must be 17 to drive on a public road (16 for a moped or light quad bike).
review.note: The minimum application age of 15 years 9 months is stated, but the text does not give the driving ages of 17, or 16 for a moped or light quad bike; it only says there are different rules depending on age and vehicle.
review.quote: be at least 15 years and 9 months old

review.name: Provisional Driving Licence
review.graph: Must have been resident in Great Britain for at least 185 days in the last 12 months.
review.note: The text requires permission to live in Great Britain for at least 185 days, not actual residence for 185 days in the last 12 months.
review.quote: have been given permission to live in Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales) for at least 185 days

review.name: Provisional Driving Licence
review.graph: Must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away (with glasses or contact lenses if worn). Certain medical conditions must be declared.
review.note: The 20-metre number plate test is stated, but the text does not mention wearing glasses or contact lenses or declaring medical conditions.
review.quote: be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away

review.name: Renew driving licence at 70
review.graph: Must confirm at renewal that eyesight meets minimum standard and no medical condition prevents driving. DVLA may require medical evidence if a condition has been declared.
review.note: The eyesight and fitness-to-drive conditions are stated, but the text only says medical details may need checking, not that DVLA may require medical evidence for a declared condition.
review.quote: you meet the minimum eyesight requirement you are not prevented from driving for any reason

review.name: Renew driving licence
review.graph: Must hold a valid UK driving licence. Photo expiry renewal applies every 10 years for drivers under 70.
review.note: The text gives the 10-year photocard renewal and says there's a different way to renew if you're 70 or over, but it never requires holding a valid UK driving licence; it lists being a resident of Great Britain and not being disqualified from driving instead.
review.quote: You must renew a photocard licence every 10 years

review.name: Make a SORN
review.graph: Registered keeper of a vehicle whose tax has lapsed or is about to lapse, and which will be kept off public roads.
review.note: The text supports keeping the vehicle off the road, and 'registered in your name' for online applications, but it does not make lapsed or soon-to-lapse tax a condition: a SORN can start whether or not the tax has expired, and you get a refund of remaining tax.
review.quote: Tell DVLA you’re taking your vehicle off the road, for example if you’re keeping it in a garage.

review.name: Tax your vehicle
review.graph: Must have a V5C log book in your name (or the green new keeper slip if recently purchased), a valid MOT, and valid insurance before taxing.
review.note: The text supports the V5C in your name or green new keeper slip, and a valid MOT, but a recent tax reminder letter is also accepted, and valid insurance is only required for Post Office applications in Northern Ireland, not in general.
review.quote: You might also need to show evidence of an MOT (it must be valid when the tax starts).

review.name: Driving Test (practical)
review.graph: A valid theory test pass certificate (valid for 2 years from the date of the theory test) is required to book.
review.note: The text says you need a theory test pass before booking, but it never says the certificate is valid for 2 years.
review.quote: You must pass your theory test before you can book your driving test.

review.name: Attendance Allowance
review.graph: Must have reached State Pension age (66 or over).
review.note: The text requires State Pension age but never gives the age as 66 or any other number.
review.quote: You can get Attendance Allowance if you’ve reached State Pension age

review.name: Repay a benefit overpayment
review.graph: Must have been notified by DWP of a benefit overpayment.
review.note: The text says the benefit office will send a letter about the overpayment, but it never makes that letter a condition of repaying: it tells people to report overpayments themselves, and it only names DWP as the sender for Debt Management and estate letters.
review.quote: You’ll get a letter to let you know that you’ve been overpaid.

review.name: Bereavement Support Payment
review.graph: Must have been under State Pension age (66) at the time of the partner's death.
review.note: The text requires being under State Pension age when the partner died, but it never gives the age as 66.
review.quote: When your partner died, you must have been: under State Pension age

review.name: Bereavement Support Payment
review.graph: Deceased must have paid at least 25 weeks of Class 1 or 2 NI contributions, or died from a work-related accident or disease.
review.note: The text gives both routes (Class 1 or 2 contributions, or a work-related accident or disease) but only says 'a certain amount' and never states the 25-week threshold.
review.quote: paid a certain amount of Class 1 or Class 2 National Insurance contributions in any one tax year since 6 April 1975 died because of an accident at work or a disease caused by work

review.name: Disability Living Allowance (Child)
review.graph: Must be in England, Wales or Northern Ireland (Scotland uses Child Disability Payment).
review.note: The text requires the child to be living in England or Wales and sends Scotland to Child Disability Payment, but it sends Northern Ireland to a separate NI scheme, so it does not directly name Northern Ireland as a qualifying place for this claim.
review.quote: be living in England or Wales when you claim (unless you’re eligible to claim from abroad)

review.name: Funeral Expenses Payment
review.graph: You or your partner must be receiving Universal Credit, Pension Credit, Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Housing Benefit, or the child tax credit and working tax credit element at the maximum rate.
review.note: The text lists Universal Credit, income-related ESA, Pension Credit and Housing Benefit, but not Income Support, income-based JSA or the tax credit routes.
review.quote: You (or your partner) must get one or more of the following: Universal Credit income-related Employment and Support Allowance Pension Credit Housing Benefit

review.name: Funeral Expenses Payment
review.graph: You are responsible for the funeral costs of a partner, close relative, or close friend where there is no other close relative able to pay.
review.note: The text covers partners and close relatives or friends, and says another close relative in work or not on benefits may block a claim, but it frames this as 'arranging' the funeral and allows relatives or friends only if the deceased had no partner or the partner cannot claim.
review.quote: If a close relative of the deceased (such as a sibling or parent) is in work or not getting a qualifying benefit, you might not get a Funeral Expenses Payment.

review.name: Mandatory Reconsideration
review.graph: A DWP benefit decision has been received (e.g. UC, JSA, ESA, PIP award or change). Mandatory Reconsideration must happen before a tribunal appeal.
review.note: The text covers benefit decisions including UC, JSA, ESA and PIP and says an appeal needs a mandatory reconsideration notice first, but it never names DWP and also says 'Others can go straight to an appeal', so mandatory reconsideration is not always required before an appeal.
review.quote: You cannot appeal to the Social Security and Child Support Tribunal until you get your mandatory reconsideration notice.

review.name: New Style ESA
review.graph: Must have paid sufficient Class 1 or Class 2 NI contributions in both of the last two complete tax years.
review.note: The text requires enough NI contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years, and says credits count, but it never names Class 1 or Class 2 contributions or says they must be paid in both of the last two complete tax years.
review.quote: paid enough National Insurance contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years - National Insurance credits also count

review.name: New Style Jobseeker's Allowance
review.graph: Must have paid Class 1 NI contributions in both of the last two complete tax years before the year of claim.
review.note: The text says Class 1 contributions for the previous 2 tax years are usually needed, but it lets credits count for one year, and its example (claims up to 3 January 2026 use 2022-23 and 2023-24) shows these are not always the last two complete tax years before the claim.
review.quote: To be eligible you must usually have made Class 1 National Insurance contributions for the previous 2 tax years. National Insurance credits can count for one of these years if you did not pay National Insurance contributions.

review.name: National Insurance number
review.graph: Must have the right to work in the UK, evidenced by a Biometric Residence Permit, eVisa, or other valid leave to remain.
review.note: The text requires the right to live and work in the UK, but it mentions BRPs and eVisas only as places to find an existing NI number, not as evidence of the right to work, and it never mentions 'other valid leave to remain'.
review.quote: you must have the right to live and work in the UK

review.name: National Insurance number
review.graph: UK citizens are automatically assigned one — applies mainly to non-UK nationals who have arrived to work or study.
review.note: The text says UK residents are normally sent a number automatically only if a Child Benefit claim was made, not UK citizens in general, and it does not say the service applies mainly to non-UK nationals arriving to work or study.
review.quote: You’ll normally be sent a National Insurance number in the 3 months before your 16th birthday if both the following are true: you live in the UK a parent or guardian has filled in a Child Benefit claim form for you

review.name: Pension Credit
review.graph: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66).
review.note: The text requires State Pension age but never says that age is currently 66.
review.quote: You must live in England, Scotland or Wales and have reached State Pension age to qualify for Pension Credit.

review.name: Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
review.graph: Must be aged 16 to 64 (under State Pension age). Those over 65 who did not have PIP before should claim Attendance Allowance instead.
review.note: The text says you must be 16 or over and usually under State Pension age, and that people over State Pension age can apply for Attendance Allowance, but it never gives the figures 64 or 65 (it says 'State Pension age'); it also lets people claim if they got PIP or ADP in the last 12 months.
review.quote: You also usually need to be under State Pension age to make a new PIP claim.

review.name: Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
review.graph: Long-term physical or mental health condition or disability affecting daily living or mobility. Must have had difficulties for at least 3 months and expect them to continue for at least 9 months.
review.note: The text requires a long-term condition and difficulties expected to last at least 12 months from when they started, but it does not state the split into 3 months already experienced plus 9 months expected.
review.quote: you expect the difficulties to last for at least 12 months from when they started

review.name: Support for Mortgage Interest
review.graph: Must be a homeowner with a mortgage, loan or other charge on the property.
review.note: The text requires a mortgage or home improvement loan on the home you live in, but it never mentions any 'other charge' on the property.
review.quote: you must have a mortgage or home improvement loan for the property you live in

review.name: State Pension claim
review.graph: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66 for men and women).
review.note: The text says you must reach State Pension age, but it never says that age is currently 66 for men and women.
review.quote: You’ll be able to claim the new State Pension when you reach State Pension age

review.name: State Pension claim
review.graph: Need at least 10 qualifying years of NI contributions or credits to receive any State Pension; 35 years for the full amount.
review.note: The text confirms that 10 qualifying years (from contributions or credits) are needed for any new State Pension, but it gives 35 years for the full rate only for records started after April 2016, and says people who were contracted out usually need more than 35.
review.quote: If your National Insurance record started after April 2016 you will need 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of new State Pension.

review.name: Tell Us Once
review.graph: Death registered in England, Scotland or most of Wales (not available in all areas).
review.note: The text makes eligibility depend on where the person lived (England, Scotland or Wales), with the death registered or reported to a coroner; it does not say the death must be registered in those countries, and it gives no limit to 'most of Wales' or says the service is unavailable in some areas.
review.quote: You can use Tell Us Once if the person who died was living in England, Scotland or Wales.

review.name: UC Carer element
review.graph: Eligible for Carer's Allowance (caring 35+ hours/week for someone on qualifying disability benefit).
review.note: The text requires 35+ hours of care a week for someone on a listed disability benefit, but it does not make Carer's Allowance eligibility a condition; it only says 'You may also be eligible for Carer's Allowance'.
review.quote: You need to provide care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

review.name: UC limited capability element
review.graph: Health condition or disability that limits or prevents capacity for work, determined by a Work Capability Assessment.
review.note: The text says the extra amount is for a health condition or disability that stops you working and mentions it being 'assessed', but it only names the Work Capability Assessment for students, not as how this element is decided.
review.quote: You might get an extra monthly amount if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

review.name: Universal Credit
review.graph: Must be habitually resident in the UK.
review.note: The text only says you must live in the UK. It never uses the phrase 'habitually resident' or mentions a habitual residence test.
review.quote: live in the UK

review.name: Voluntary National Insurance contributions (Class 3)
review.graph: You have gaps in your National Insurance record that would increase your State Pension if filled.
review.note: The text says you need gaps in your record to pay (unless an exception applies), but it does not require that filling them would increase your State Pension; it only tells you to check whether you would benefit.
review.quote: do not have gaps in your National Insurance record

review.name: Voluntary National Insurance contributions (Class 3)
review.graph: Under State Pension age, or within the window where contributions still count.
review.note: The text sets no upper age limit and lets people over State Pension age pay Class 3; the only window it gives is the 6-year deadline for past years, so the 'under State Pension age' part is not a condition the text states.
review.quote: If you’ve reached State Pension age and want to fill in gaps in your National Insurance record you can pay: Class 3 contributions

review.name: Winter Fuel Payment
review.graph: Must usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, and be there in the qualifying week of 21 to 27 September 2026.
review.note: The text supports the usual-residence rule and names 21 to 27 September 2026 as the qualifying week, but it never says you must be physically in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during that week. It only excludes visitors who usually live somewhere else.
review.quote: You can get a Winter Fuel Payment if you were born on or before 27 June 1960 and usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

review.name: Get a rod fishing licence
review.graph: One licence covers England and Wales, including all of the Border Esk. Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate arrangements.
review.note: The text confirms the licence covers Wales and the whole Border Esk, and that Scotland and Northern Ireland have different rules, but it excludes the River Tweed from England's coverage, which the criterion leaves out.
review.quote: England (except the River Tweed) Wales the Border Esk region, including the parts of the river that are in Scotland

review.name: Emergency travel document
review.graph: Must be outside the UK without a valid passport.
review.note: The text requires being outside the UK and unable to use your UK passport for specific listed reasons, some of which (full, or held by HM Passport Office or an embassy) do not mean the passport is invalid, so 'without a valid passport' is only a loose match.
review.quote: your UK passport has been lost, stolen, damaged, is full, has recently expired or is with HM Passport Office or a foreign embassy

review.name: Obtain death certificates
review.graph: Death must have been registered before certified copies can be ordered.
review.note: The text assumes the death has already been registered, since it talks about ordering copies from the office where the death was registered, but it never says registration is required before copies can be ordered.
review.quote: You can also order certificates from the local register office where the birth, death or marriage was registered.

review.name: Give notice of marriage
review.graph: Both parties must be 18 or over (16-17 with parental consent in exceptional circumstances).
review.note: The text gives 18 or over but says nothing about 16-17 year olds marrying with parental consent.
review.quote: You can get married or form a civil partnership in England or Wales if you’re: 18 or over

review.name: Marriage / CP certificate
review.graph: Must have legally married or formed a civil partnership in England or Wales.
review.note: The text limits the service to marriages or civil partnerships registered in England and Wales, but it never says the applicant must be one of the people who married or formed the partnership; it also mentions family tree research, which suggests other people can order.
review.quote: get a copy of a birth, adoption, death, marriage or civil partnership certificate in England and Wales

review.name: Register the birth
review.graph: Deadline is 42 days in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 21 days in Scotland.
review.note: The 42-day deadline for England, Wales and Northern Ireland is stated, but the text only says Scotland has different rules and never gives a 21-day deadline.
review.quote: All births in England, Wales and Northern Ireland must be registered within 42 days of the child being born.

review.name: Register the death
review.graph: A person has died in England or Wales.
review.note: The text covers registering a death in the UK or abroad, but it never names England or Wales as the place where the death must have happened.
review.quote: Find out how to register a death in the UK or abroad.

review.name: Social Security & Child Support Tribunal
review.graph: Mandatory Reconsideration must have been completed and the outcome confirmed in a Mandatory Reconsideration Notice from DWP.
review.note: The text requires a mandatory reconsideration notice only 'usually': it allows an exception when the decision letter says you can appeal straight away, and it never says the notice comes from DWP.
review.quote: You’ll need to provide your mandatory reconsideration notice when applying. If you do not need a mandatory reconsideration your decision letter will say why.

review.name: Child Arrangements Order
review.graph: Separated parents with children under 16 (or up to 18 if the order already exists).
review.note: The text covers separated parents with children, but it gives no age limit, so neither 'under 16' nor 'up to 18 if the order already exists' is stated.
review.quote: You can choose how to make arrangements for looking after your children if you separate from your partner.

review.name: Divorce application (D8)
review.graph: Must have been married or in a civil partnership for at least 1 year.
review.note: The text gives the over-one-year rule for marriage only; for civil partnerships it points to a separate guide and does not set out the civil partnership route.
review.quote: you’ve been married for over a year

review.name: Employment Tribunal claim
review.graph: Must have an employment dispute — unfair dismissal requires at least 2 years' service; discrimination claims have no service requirement.
review.note: The text says claims can be about unfair dismissal or discrimination, but it never mentions the 2-year service requirement for unfair dismissal or that discrimination claims have no service requirement.
review.quote: Unlawful treatment can include: unfair dismissal discrimination at work breach of contract unauthorised deductions from your pay

review.name: Employment Tribunal claim
review.graph: Must have an Acas EC certificate (early conciliation must be attempted first).
review.note: The text says a certificate is usually needed, but it lists exceptions (such as interim relief claims or when the respondent has already notified Acas) and says you can choose not to take part in conciliation and still get the certificate, so attempting conciliation is not strictly required.
review.quote: You'll usually need an early conciliation certificate for each respondent before you make a claim .

review.name: Appeal to Immigration Tribunal
review.graph: Must have received a Home Office refusal that explicitly grants a right of appeal.
review.note: The text requires a legal right of appeal against a Home Office decision, but it only says the decision letter will 'usually' tell you whether you have that right, not that it must explicitly grant it; it also lists decisions other than refusals, such as revocation and deportation.
review.quote: You can only appeal to the tribunal if you have the legal right to appeal - you’ll usually be told if you do in your decision letter.

review.name: Legal Aid application
review.graph: Disposable income must be below £2,657/month and disposable capital below £8,000 (thresholds vary by case type).
review.note: The text gives £2,657 a month and £8,000 in assets, but as gross joint income before tax (or a qualifying benefit) and total assets, not 'disposable' income or capital; it names exceptions but does not say thresholds vary by case type.
review.quote: have a joint monthly income of £2,657 or less (before tax and other deductions)

review.name: Apply for probate
review.graph: Person has died leaving assets held in their sole name.
review.note: The text covers dealing with the estate of someone who has died, and says jointly owned assets pass to the surviving owners, but it never says the assets must be held in the person's sole name.
review.quote: owned shares or money with others - this automatically passes to the surviving owners

review.name: Appeal to Tax Tribunal
review.graph: Must have received a formal decision from HMRC and exercised the right to request HMRC review first (in most cases).
review.note: The text says you must first appeal to HMRC for direct tax decisions, and for refusals to return seized goods. It presents an HMRC review as optional ('You can ask for a review'), and says indirect tax decisions can usually go straight to the tribunal, so it does not support a review being required in most cases.
review.quote: You must appeal direct tax decisions to HMRC before you can appeal to the tribunal. You can usually appeal indirect tax decisions straight to the tribunal.

review.name: Urgent passport application
review.graph: Must be a British national with imminent international travel.
review.note: The text bases eligibility on needing a passport faster than the standard service and never mentions being a British national or requires imminent international travel; it only says who cannot use the service (first adult passport, applicants outside the UK).
review.quote: You can pay to get a passport urgently if you think the standard service will take too long.

review.name: Cancel Marriage Allowance
review.graph: Previously claimed Marriage Allowance and relationship has now ended (separated, divorced, or partner died).
review.note: The text lists divorce, dissolving a civil partnership and legal separation as reasons to cancel, but it does not list a partner's death as one. It covers death separately, saying Personal Allowances change automatically, and it specifies legal separation rather than separation in general.
review.quote: your relationship ends - because you've divorced, ended ('dissolved') your civil partnership or legally separated

review.name: Carer's Credit
review.graph: Not already receiving NI credits through Carer's Allowance, UC, or earnings above the Lower Earnings Limit.
review.note: The text says people on Carer's Allowance get credits automatically and need not apply, but it does not mention Universal Credit or earnings above the Lower Earnings Limit.
review.quote: get Carer’s Allowance or Carer Support Payment - you’ll automatically get credits

review.name: Child Benefit
review.graph: High Income Child Benefit Charge claws back the payment if either partner's individual adjusted net income is over £60,000; the charge equals the full benefit at £80,000 or more. It does not affect eligibility.
review.note: The text covers the charge, individual adjusted net income, the full clawback at £20,000 above the threshold, and keeping the other benefits, but never names the threshold as £60,000: that figure appears only in an opt-out example about 'annual income', so £80,000 is inferred, not stated.
review.quote: If either you or your partner has an individual income of £20,000 or more above the threshold (£10,000 or more before April 2024), you’ll be charged the same amount as you make through Child Benefit payments.

review.name: Child Benefit transfer
review.graph: Child has moved to live primarily with a different parent after separation.
review.note: The text covers families splitting up with a child living with an ex-partner, and says you can change who gets Child Benefit, but it never says that a child moving to live mainly with the other parent is a reason to transfer the claim.
review.quote: If you have 2 children and one lives with you and the other lives with someone else (for example, your ex-partner), you’ll each get £27.05 a week.

review.name: Child Benefit transfer
review.graph: Parents have separated and current Child Benefit claimant is no longer the main carer.
review.note: The text describes how to transfer a claim and mentions families splitting up, but it does not tie a transfer to the current claimant no longer being the main carer after separation.
review.quote: Contact the Child Benefit Office if you want someone else to claim Child Benefit, for example, your spouse or partner. After you’ve done this, tell the other person to make a new claim.

review.name: Register for Corporation Tax
review.graph: All UK-registered limited companies, regardless of profitability or size.
review.note: The text limits the duty to limited companies that are active and within the charge to Corporation Tax, not all UK-registered limited companies, and it does not say that profitability or size is irrelevant.
review.quote: You must tell HMRC within 3 months of starting your tax accounting period if your limited company is within the charge of Corporation Tax and is now active.

review.name: Register for Corporation Tax
review.graph: Requires Companies House registration to be in place first.
review.note: Asking for a company registration number in the written application suggests the company is already registered, but the text never says Companies House registration must be in place before registering for Corporation Tax.
review.quote: the company’s name and registration number

review.name: Marriage Allowance
review.graph: One partner must have income below the Personal Allowance (£12,570/year). The other must be a basic-rate (20%) taxpayer.
review.note: The text says the lower earner's income must be below the Personal Allowance (usually £12,570) and the partner must pay basic rate, but it never gives the 20% rate, and in Scotland it also allows the starter and intermediate rates.
review.quote: you do not pay Income Tax or your income is below your Personal Allowance (usually £12,570) your partner pays Income Tax at the basic rate

review.name: Making Tax Digital enrolment
review.graph: Mandatory for all VAT-registered businesses. Phased in for income tax self-assessment from 2026.
review.note: The text supports MTD for all VAT-registered businesses, though it allows for exemptions, but says nothing about a phase-in for income tax self-assessment from 2026.
review.quote: All VAT registered businesses should now be signed up for Making Tax Digital for VAT.

review.name: Obtain P45 from employer
review.graph: Must have been employed under PAYE and left that employment.
review.note: The text says you must be an employee who has left the job, but it never says the employment has to be under PAYE.
review.quote: When you leave a job, your employer should give you a P45 form

review.name: Register as employer (PAYE)
review.graph: Taking on an employee who will be paid £96 or more a week, get expenses or benefits, get a pension, has had another job, or has received JSA, ESA or Incapacity Benefit (including a director employing only themselves).
review.note: The text says you must register when you start employing staff, including a director employing only themselves, but it never mentions the £96 weekly threshold, expenses or benefits, pensions, previous jobs, or JSA/ESA/Incapacity Benefit.
review.quote: You must register even if you’re only employing yourself, for example as the only director of a limited company .

review.name: Register as sole trader
review.graph: Has started to trade as a sole trader (self-employed), earning income from their own business.
review.note: The text links registering to trading as a self-employed sole trader, but the stated trigger is earning more than £1,000 in a tax year, which the criterion leaves out, and the text also says you can choose to register earlier.
review.quote: You can start trading straight away without registering. However, you must register for Self Assessment as a sole trader if you earn more than £1,000 in a tax year (from 6 April to 5 April).

review.name: Stamp Duty Land Tax return
review.graph: Any purchase of land or property in England (or Northern Ireland) — thresholds vary for first-time buyers, additional properties, etc.
review.note: The text limits SDLT to purchases over a certain price, with different rates for first-time buyers and additional properties, and it lists exemptions where no return is needed (for example a freehold under £40,000), so it does not support 'any purchase'.
review.quote: You must pay Stamp Duty Land Tax ( SDLT ) if you buy a property or land over a certain price in England and Northern Ireland.

review.name: Shared Parental Leave & Pay
review.graph: Mother must be eligible for SMP or Maternity Allowance for SPL to be available.
review.note: The text links ShPP to reducing SMP or Maternity Allowance, but it never says the mother must be eligible for SMP or Maternity Allowance for SPL (the leave) to be available.
review.quote: take less than the 39 weeks of maternity or adoption pay (or Maternity Allowance) and use the rest as ShPP

review.name: Statutory Paternity Pay
review.graph: Continuously employed with the same employer for at least 26 weeks and earning at or above the Lower Earnings Limit.
review.note: The text supports 26 weeks' continuous employment and an earnings threshold of £129 a week, but it never mentions the 'Lower Earnings Limit', so it does not show that this threshold is the one the criterion names.
review.quote: earn an average of at least £129 a week (before tax) give the correct notice have been continuously employed by your employer for at least 26 weeks

review.name: Statutory Sick Pay (SSP)
review.graph: Must be classed as an employee (including agency workers) and have done some work for the employer; self-employed individuals are not eligible.
review.note: The text requires employee status and some work done for the employer, and says agency workers 'may be entitled', but it never says self-employed people are not eligible.
review.quote: be classed as an employee have done some work for your employer

review.name: Tax-Free Childcare account
review.graph: Provider must be approved childcare and signed up to Tax-Free Childcare. Check registration with Ofsted or a registered childminder agency in England, Care Inspectorate Wales, the Care Inspectorate in Scotland, or the local early years team in Northern Ireland.
review.note: The text says the provider must be approved childcare and signed up to Tax-Free Childcare, but it does not name Ofsted, Care Inspectorate Wales, the Care Inspectorate in Scotland or the Northern Ireland early years team as ways to check registration.
review.quote: You must use an ‘approved childcare’ provider to get Tax-Free Childcare

review.name: Income tax refund (P50)
review.graph: Unemployed for 4 weeks or more, not claiming taxable state benefits, and not returning to work or starting a taxable pension in the same tax year — if you expect to start a new job within 4 weeks, your new employer will make any repayment through your salary instead.
review.note: The text supports the 4-week unemployment, the no-taxable-benefits condition and the new-job-within-4-weeks exclusion, but it does not make 'not returning to work or starting a taxable pension in the same tax year' a combined requirement: 'do not expect to go back to work' is listed as a separate example, and other taxable income or a pension is only something to check.
review.quote: have been unemployed for 4 weeks or more and are not claiming taxable state benefits

review.name: VAT registration
review.graph: Taxable turnover has exceeded or is expected to exceed £90,000 in a rolling 12-month period.
review.note: The £90,000 threshold over the last 12 months is stated, but the text puts the expected-turnover test on the next 30 days, not a rolling 12-month period as the criterion says.
review.quote: your total taxable turnover for the last 12 months goes over £90,000 (the VAT threshold) you expect your taxable turnover to go over £90,000 in the next 30 days

review.name: Biometric Residence Permit
review.graph: Granted a UK visa or leave to remain for more than 6 months.
review.note: The text links BRPs to being granted permission to live or work in the UK, but it never mentions the 'more than 6 months' length condition, and it adds a cut-off of on or before 31 October 2024.
review.quote: You might have a BRP if you were granted permission to live or work in the UK on or before 31 October 2024.

review.name: British citizenship (naturalisation)
review.graph: Must be of good character (no serious criminal record) and demonstrate knowledge of English, Welsh or Scottish Gaelic.
review.note: The text requires good character and knowledge of English, Welsh or Scottish Gaelic, but it never defines good character as having no serious criminal record.
review.quote: prove your knowledge of English , Welsh or Scottish Gaelic have passed the life in the UK test intend to continue living in the UK be of good character

review.name: Citizenship ceremony
review.graph: Adults aged 18 and over must attend in person. Children under 18 can be included on a parent's ceremony.
review.note: The text says people aged 18 or over must attend, but it says nothing about children under 18 being included on a parent's ceremony.
review.quote: You need to attend a citizenship ceremony if you’re 18 or over and have successfully applied to become a British citizen.

review.name: Report an error with your eVisa
review.graph: Has a UKVI account, including one the Home Office set up that you have never been able to sign in to.
review.note: The text covers the case of an account the Home Office set up that you have never signed in to, but it never says a UKVI account is required for every case, such as reporting wrong eVisa details.
review.quote: the Home Office set up your UKVI account and you’ve never been able to sign in to it

review.name: Immigration fee waiver
review.graph: Must demonstrate that payment of the visa fee would leave you (or your family) destitute or at risk of destitution.
review.note: The text describes not being able to afford the fee because you lack housing or essential living costs, which is close to destitution, but it never says 'destitute' or 'at risk of destitution', and it adds a separate route: very low income where paying would harm your child's wellbeing.
review.quote: You can apply for a fee waiver if you cannot afford to pay the fee because you: do not have a place to live in the UK and you cannot afford one have a place to live but cannot afford essential living costs like food or heating

review.name: Immigration fee waiver
review.graph: Must be applying for a qualifying leave to remain or citizenship application.
review.note: The text supports applications for permission to stay (leave to remain) on certain routes, but it says nothing about citizenship applications.
review.quote: You can apply for a fee waiver if you’re applying for permission to stay in the UK.

review.name: Indefinite Leave to Remain
review.graph: Met the qualifying period of lawful residence (usually 5 years on eligible visa such as Skilled Worker, Family, or Tier routes).
review.note: The usual 5-year period is stated for work visas such as Skilled Worker and Tier 2, but the text gives no qualifying period for the Family route, and Tier 1 can be 2 or 3 years.
review.quote: You must usually have lived and worked in the UK for 5 years.

review.name: Life in the UK test
review.graph: Applying for Indefinite Leave to Remain or British citizenship (by naturalisation, as spouse/civil partner of a British citizen, or as an Irish citizen).
review.note: The text covers citizenship and settlement applications in general, but it does not name the specific routes: naturalisation, spouse/civil partner of a British citizen, or Irish citizen.
review.quote: You need to take the test as part of your application for British citizenship or settlement in the UK.

review.name: Student visa
review.graph: Must be a non-British, non-Irish national without leave to remain that covers the course.
review.note: The text says people with EU Settlement Scheme status do not need a visa, but it never says applicants must be non-British or non-Irish nationals, and it has no general rule about already holding leave that covers the course.
review.quote: If you have settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme, you do not need to apply for a visa.

review.name: View or prove your immigration status
review.graph: Must have a UKVI account with an eVisa or EU Settlement Scheme status.
review.note: The text says you need a UKVI account and an eVisa, but it never mentions EU Settlement Scheme status as another qualifying route.
review.quote: You’ll need the details you use to sign in to your UKVI account.

review.name: Visa / leave to enter
review.graph: Non-UK, non-Irish national wishing to enter the UK (some nationalities require visa; others may enter visa-free for short stays).
review.note: The text covers people who are not British or Irish and says they may need a visa or an ETA, but it never says outright that some nationalities can enter visa-free for short stays.
review.quote: Check if you need a UK Visa, electronic travel authorisation (ETA) or get access to an eVisa to prove your immigration status if you’re not a British citizen or Irish national

review.name: Visa / leave to enter
review.graph: Must apply for the specific visa type matching the purpose of entry (Skilled Worker, Student, Family Visa, etc.).
review.note: The text groups visa types by purpose (work, study, family) and names Skilled Worker and Student visas, but it does not say you must apply for the visa that matches your purpose of entry.
review.quote: Work in the UK Skilled Worker visa, Graduate visa, other work visas, right to work Study in the UK Student visas

review.name: Apply for bankruptcy
review.graph: Must live or have a business in England or Wales.
review.note: The text limits the service to England and Wales but does not say the applicant must live or have a business there.
review.quote: Use this service to apply for bankruptcy in England and Wales.

review.name: Breathing Space (debt respite scheme)
review.graph: Must engage with an FCA-authorised debt advice provider who applies on the person's behalf.
review.note: The text says a debt adviser applies for you, but it does not say the adviser must be FCA-authorised; FCA authorisation is mentioned only for Debt Management Plan companies.
review.quote: To apply for the ‘Breathing Space’ scheme, you need to talk to a debt adviser. They will submit an application on your behalf if it’s the right thing to do.

review.name: Debt Relief Order (DRO)
review.graph: Must live or have been living in England or Wales.
review.note: The text limits the test to the last 3 years and also accepts having worked in England and Wales; the criterion gives no time limit and leaves out the work route.
review.quote: you’ve lived or worked in England and Wales within the last 3 years

review.name: Free bus pass
review.graph: Must have reached State Pension age (currently 66). Some disabled people may also qualify before this age.
review.note: The text supports State Pension age for England and links to a disabled person's bus pass, but it never gives the figure 66, and it says Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and London use age 60.
review.quote: In England you can get a bus pass for free travel when you reach the State Pension age .

review.name: Carer's Assessment
review.graph: Any adult (18+) who provides regular and substantial unpaid care for someone with a disability, health condition, or frailty.
review.note: The text supports the age (over 18) and regular care for someone who is ill, older or disabled ("looking after someone regularly because they're ill, they're an older person or they're disabled"), but it never says the care must be "substantial" or "unpaid".
review.quote: A carer's assessment is free and anyone over 18 can ask for one.

review.name: Child performance licence
review.graph: Applies in England, Scotland and Wales; Northern Ireland has separate rules.
review.note: The text says Northern Ireland has different rules, but it never names England, Scotland and Wales as the places where this applies.
review.quote: The rules are different in Northern Ireland .

review.name: Council Tax Disability Reduction
review.graph: A disabled person must live in the property. The property must have been adapted or have features essential for the disabled person's needs.
review.note: The text says a disabled person must live in the property and that it must have features needed for them (an extra room or wheelchair space), but it never mentions the property being 'adapted'.
review.quote: The property must be the main home of at least 1 disabled person.

review.name: Council Tax Disability Reduction
review.graph: Property must have at least one of: a room mainly used by the disabled person (not a bedroom, bathroom or kitchen); an extra bathroom or kitchen for the disabled person; extra space inside for wheelchair use.
review.note: The extra bathroom or kitchen and the wheelchair space are stated, but the text only says 'other room that you need', not a room 'mainly used' by the disabled person, and it does not exclude bedrooms.
review.quote: an extra bathroom, kitchen or other room that you need for the disabled person extra space inside the property for using a wheelchair

review.name: Council Tax Reduction
review.graph: Low income or receiving means-tested benefits such as Universal Credit, Income Support, Pension Credit.
review.note: The text mentions low income and claiming benefits in general, but it never names Universal Credit, Income Support or Pension Credit as qualifying benefits.
review.quote: You could be eligible if you’re on a low income or claim benefits.

review.name: Council Tax Reduction
review.graph: Must be liable for Council Tax at that address.
review.note: The text suggests the applicant has a Council Tax bill and can own or rent, but it never says they must be liable for Council Tax at that address.
review.quote: You’ll get a discount on your bill if you’re eligible.

review.name: Council Tax single person discount
review.graph: Now living alone as the only adult (18+) in the property, following bereavement or separation.
review.note: The text supports the discount for living on your own, and it counts adults as people aged 18 or over, but it never says this has to follow bereavement or separation.
review.quote: You’ll get 25% off your bill if you pay Council Tax and either: you live on your own everyone else in your home is disregarded

review.name: Disabled Facilities Grant
review.graph: Property in England where the disabled person lives, whether owned, rented privately, or from a housing association.
review.note: Owners, tenants and landlords can apply, but the text does not say private or housing association tenancies specifically, and it gives grant amounts for Wales and Northern Ireland as well as England, so it does not limit the grant to England.
review.quote: The person who submits the application must be either the: owner tenant landlord

review.name: Electoral roll update
review.graph: Must be 16 or over to register (18 to vote in most elections).
review.note: The text gives 16 as the minimum age to register in England and Northern Ireland but 14 in Scotland and Wales, and it never states that the voting age is 18.
review.quote: If you live in England or Northern Ireland You must be aged 16 or over to register.

review.name: Electoral roll update
review.graph: British, Irish, or qualifying Commonwealth citizen (EU citizens can vote in local elections).
review.note: The text supports registration for British, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens, but it does not say that EU citizens can vote in local elections; it only lists certain EU citizens who can register.
review.quote: You can register to vote if you’re a British citizen or an Irish citizen. You can also register if you have permission (or do not need permission) to enter or stay in the UK, Channel Islands or Isle of Man and you’re: a Commonwealth citizen

review.name: Free School Meals
review.graph: Child is of compulsory school age and attends a state-funded school in England.
review.note: The text covers England and government-funded schools, but it never makes compulsory school age a requirement; it says children younger than compulsory school age may also qualify, though the full condition is cut off.
review.quote: Your child will be able to get free school meals if they’re in a government-funded school and in:

review.name: Apply for a proxy vote
review.graph: Typical reasons include being at work, abroad, or unable to attend due to disability or illness.
review.note: The text gives the general reason (you cannot go to the polling station) and covers applicants who live abroad, but it never names being at work, disability or illness as reasons.
review.quote: You can get someone else to vote on your behalf (a proxy) if you cannot go to the polling station in person.

review.name: Public film or TV screening permissions
review.graph: Showing films or TV programmes in a public or communal setting: cinema club, hotel, pub, outdoor event, community hall, retail display, or staff room.
review.note: The text covers staff rooms, hotels, retail venues, one-off events and film clubs, but it never names pubs, outdoor events or community halls.
review.quote: Public spaces or events may include: staff rooms common areas for guests or passengers (for example receptions or lounge spaces) bedrooms in hotels and guesthouses retail and entertainment venues one-off events film clubs community cinemas

review.name: School place application
review.graph: Local authority area determines which schools are offered. Catchment area, siblings, faith criteria vary by school.
review.note: The text says you apply through your local council, and that you can apply for schools in other council areas, but it does not say the local authority area decides which schools are offered, and it does not mention catchment, sibling or faith criteria.
review.quote: You apply through your local council even if you’re applying for schools in another council area.

review.name: Short-term let licence (Scotland)
review.graph: Must own or manage a residential property being let for short-term stays.
review.note: The text covers letting out accommodation to guests on a temporary basis, but it never says the applicant must own or manage the property or that the property must be residential.
review.quote: A short-term let licence gives you legal permission to let out accommodation to guests who stay on a temporary basis.

review.name: Street trading licence
review.graph: Selling goods or services from a street or public place in England and Wales.
review.note: The text covers trading in the street in England and Wales, but it never mentions a 'public place' or says 'goods or services'.
review.quote: You may need to get a licence to trade in the street in England and Wales

review.name: Voter Authority Certificate
review.graph: Must be eligible to vote (registered on the electoral roll as a British, Irish, or qualifying Commonwealth citizen).
review.note: The text requires registration to vote but does not mention British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizenship.
review.quote: You must be registered to vote to apply.

review.name: Voter Authority Certificate
review.graph: Must be registered to vote. Only needed if you do not already have an accepted form of photo ID.
review.note: The text supports the registration requirement and the point about lacking accepted photo ID, but it also lets you apply if you vote in person and no longer look like your ID photo or your ID name differs, so 'only if you do not have photo ID' is too narrow.
review.quote: You must be registered to vote to apply.

review.name: Land Registry registration (AP1)
review.graph: Any purchase of land or property in England or Wales. Also required for remortgages, transfers of equity, and first-time registrations of unregistered land.
review.note: The text covers purchases, mortgaging, adding a joint owner and first registration of unregistered land in England and Wales, but it does not name remortgages or transfers of equity, and it excludes leases with 7 years or less left, so 'any purchase' goes too far.
review.quote: You must register all land or property with HM Land Registry if you’ve: bought it been given it inherited it received it in exchange for other property or land mortgaged the property

review.name: Sign your mortgage deed
review.graph: Lender must participate in the Land Registry digital mortgage service.
review.note: The text says lenders can use HM Land Registry's digital mortgage service, but it never says the homeowner's lender must take part for the homeowner to be eligible.
review.quote: Lenders and conveyancers can use the service to create and register legal mortgages of residential property for homeowners who are remortgaging.

review.name: Care needs assessment
review.graph: Any adult who appears to need care and support due to a physical or mental condition, disability, or frailty due to age.
review.note: The text says the assessment finds out what help and support you need, but it never says it is open to any adult who appears to need care, and it names no qualifying cause such as a physical or mental condition, disability or frailty due to age.
review.quote: A health and social care assessment is carried out by social services to find out what help and support you need

review.name: NHS Continuing Healthcare (CHC)
review.graph: Primary health need assessed as complex, intense, or unpredictable — usually a progressive serious illness, terminal condition, or severe disability.
review.note: The text requires a primary health need arising from disability, accident or illness, but it does not describe that need as complex, intense or unpredictable, and it does not mention progressive serious illness or terminal conditions.
review.quote: arranged and funded solely by the NHS where an individual is found to have a primary health need

review.name: Send a fit note for an ESA claim
review.graph: Must have a health condition or disability that prevents or limits work, evidenced by a fit note from a healthcare provider.
review.note: The text says a fit note from certain healthcare professionals is needed, but it never says there must be a health condition or disability that prevents or limits work.
review.quote: Only certain healthcare professionals can give you a fit note .

review.name: Healthy Start
review.graph: England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland has Best Start Foods instead.
review.note: The text says Scotland has Best Start Foods instead, but it never says the scheme covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
review.quote: If you live in Scotland You can get help from Best Start Foods (opens in a new tab) instead.

review.name: Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC)
review.graph: Only worthwhile if you pay for NHS prescriptions — exempt groups should not apply.
review.note: The text presents the PPC as a way to cut the cost of prescriptions you pay for, but it does not mention exempt groups or say they should not apply.
review.quote: You can buy prescription prepayment certificates ( PPCs ) from the NHS which may make your prescriptions cheaper.

review.name: Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC)
review.graph: England only — prescriptions are free in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
review.note: The England-only restriction is stated, but the text does not say prescriptions are free in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
review.quote: You can only get a PPC if you live in England.

review.name: Rate Rebate
review.graph: Must be liable for domestic rates in Northern Ireland.
review.note: The text implies that claimants pay rates as homeowners or tenants, but it never states rate liability as a condition and never mentions Northern Ireland.
review.quote: You must pay your rates until you get a decision about your application for Rate Rebate.

review.name: Raise concerns about a school with Ofsted
review.graph: Must have first completed the school's own complaints procedure before escalating to Ofsted.
review.note: The text says you must already have complained to the school and the problem is still unresolved, but it never says the school's full complaints procedure has to be completed first.
review.quote: you’ve complained to the school and the problem has not been resolved

review.name: Register as a childminder with Ofsted
review.graph: England only. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have separate requirements.
review.note: The title limits the guidance to England, but the text never says that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have separate requirements.
review.quote: Become a childminder or nanny (England).

review.name: Lasting Power of Attorney
review.graph: Particularly important for those with progressive conditions (dementia, MS, Parkinson's) — must be created while mental capacity remains.
review.note: The text says the LPA must be made while the donor has mental capacity, but it never mentions progressive conditions such as dementia, MS or Parkinson's.
review.quote: You must be 18 or over and have mental capacity (the ability to make your own decisions) when you make your LPA .

review.name: Notify OPG of death
review.graph: A registered LPA exists and the donor has died.
review.note: The text says the LPA is cancelled or ends when the donor dies, but it does not say the donor's death must be reported to OPG or that the LPA must be registered for this to apply.
review.quote: OPG will cancel the LPA if the donor dies

review.name: Notify OPG of death
review.graph: Requires a registered LPA to be in place.
review.note: OPG cancelling the LPA suggests it holds a registered LPA, but the text never says outright that a registered LPA is needed before OPG can be told of a death.
review.quote: OPG will cancel the LPA if the donor dies

review.name: Carer's leave (employer)
review.graph: Must be an employee (not a worker or self-employed). Applies from the first day of employment.
review.note: The text says employees qualify from their first day of work, but it never says that workers or self-employed people are excluded.
review.quote: Employees are entitled to carer’s leave from their first day of work for their employer.

review.name: DBS check
review.graph: Role involves working with children or vulnerable adults, or is otherwise in a specified list of eligible positions (healthcare, legal, financial services roles).
review.note: The text says more detailed checks apply to certain roles, such as healthcare or childcare, and mentions care services for adults, but it does not mention legal or financial services roles or a specified list of eligible positions.
review.quote: You can request a more detailed check for certain roles, for example in healthcare or childcare.

review.name: Disabled Persons Railcard
review.graph: Receiving PIP (any component or rate), DLA, Attendance Allowance; or having epilepsy, registered severe visual/hearing impairment, or severe mental or physical disability requiring a companion.
review.note: The source backs PIP at any rate, DLA (at set rates), Attendance Allowance, epilepsy, and visual and hearing impairment, but it never mentions a severe mental or physical disability requiring a companion as a qualifying route.
review.quote: I get Personal Independence Payment (PIP) or Adult Disability Payment (ADP) at any rate

review.name: Employers' Liability Insurance
review.graph: Any business employing one or more people under a contract of service or apprenticeship.
review.note: The text says you need it once you become an employer, but it never mentions a 'contract of service or apprenticeship', and it exempts employers who only employ family members or people based outside England, Scotland and Wales, so 'any business' goes further than the text.
review.quote: You must get Employers’ Liability ( EL ) insurance: as soon as you become an employer

review.name: First Homes / Help to Buy scheme
review.graph: First-time buyer purchasing a new-build property through an eligible scheme. For First Homes: property must not exceed £250,000 after discount (£420,000 in London).
review.note: The text supports the first-time buyer requirement and the £250,000 (£420,000 London) cap after discount, but it does not limit the scheme to new-builds: it also allows resale homes bought through an estate agent from a previous First Homes buyer.
review.quote: New build First Homes cannot cost more £250,000 (or more than £420,000 if the property is in London) after the discount has been applied.

review.name: Motability scheme
review.graph: Receiving the Enhanced Rate of the Mobility Component of PIP (or equivalent: DLA highest rate mobility, AFIP or WPMS).
review.note: The text mentions only a 'qualifying mobility allowance'. It does not name the PIP enhanced mobility rate, DLA higher rate mobility, AFIP or WPMS.
review.quote: Use your qualifying mobility allowance to lease a brand-new vehicle.

review.name: Passport name change
review.graph: Name has legally changed following marriage, civil partnership, deed poll or statutory declaration.
review.note: The text says only that different rules apply if you need to change your name; it does not mention marriage, civil partnership, deed poll or statutory declaration, or require the change to be legal.
review.quote: There are different rules if your passport is lost, stolen or damaged or you need to change your name or personal details .

review.name: Pupil Premium
review.graph: Free School Meals eligibility must be registered — the school receives the funding automatically.
review.note: The text bases funding on pupils recorded as FSM-eligible in the school census, with DfE or the local authority allocating it, but it never says families must register FSM eligibility or that the school gets the money automatically.
review.quote: DfE will allocate PP grant to academies directly. This allocation will be based on FSM Ever 6 pupils, PLAC and eligible service children.

review.name: Right to work check
review.graph: Required for all new employees before they begin work. Employer faces civil penalty if not done.
review.note: The text requires the check before employment, but it only mentions a civil penalty if the employer employs an illegal worker without a correct check, not simply for skipping the check.
review.quote: You must check that a job applicant is allowed to work for you in the UK before you employ them.

review.name: Right to work check
review.graph: Non-UK/Irish nationals provide a share code via the UK Visas & Immigration online portal. British/Irish citizens present their passport.
review.note: The text mentions share codes and passports for British/Irish citizens, but it does not name a UK Visas & Immigration portal, and it lets other nationals use original documents or IDVT instead of a share code.
review.quote: British and Irish citizens cannot get an online share code to prove their right to work. You’ll need to check their original documents - for example, their passport or passport card - or use an identity service provider instead.

review.name: Statutory Redundancy Pay
review.graph: Must have been continuously employed for at least 2 years and been made compulsorily redundant.
review.note: The text supports the 2-year service requirement, but it does not say the employment must be continuous for redundancy pay, or that the redundancy must be compulsory rather than voluntary.
review.quote: You’ll normally be entitled to statutory redundancy pay if you’re an employee and you’ve been working for your current employer for 2 years or more.

review.name: Student loan repayment
review.graph: Annual income must exceed the threshold for the applicable repayment plan before any deductions are made.
review.note: The text supports the plan-specific income threshold, but it says repayments are taken whenever pay goes over the weekly or monthly threshold, even if annual income ends up below the yearly threshold (a refund can be claimed later), so 'annual' income is not strictly required before deductions are made.
review.quote: You’ll only repay your student loan when your income is over the threshold amount for your repayment plan

review.name: Student Finance (tuition fee + maintenance loans)
review.graph: Typically 18 or over (no upper age limit for loans, though some conditions apply for those over 60).
review.note: The text says there is no upper age limit for Tuition Fee Loans and grants, and limits Maintenance Loans for people aged 60 or over, but it never says students are typically 18 or over.
review.quote: There’s no upper age limit for Tuition Fee Loans or grants.

review.name: Student Finance (tuition fee + maintenance loans)
review.graph: Must be normally resident in England for 3+ years before the course starts, and a UK national or settled person.
review.note: The text requires a home in England plus 3 years' residence anywhere in the UK, Channel Islands or Isle of Man, not 3 years in England specifically, and it also covers Irish citizens alongside UK nationals and people with settled status.
review.quote: your home is in England you’ve been continuously living in the UK, Channel Islands or Isle of Man for 3 years before the first day of your first academic year

review.name: Student Finance (tuition fee + maintenance loans)
review.graph: Maintenance Loan amount is income-assessed based on household income. Tuition Fee Loan is not means-tested.

review.quote: How much you can get depends on: where you live while studying your household income your course intensity

review.name: Adult Disability Payment
review.graph: Must have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability that affects daily living or mobility for at least 13 weeks and is expected to last at least 9 more months.
review.note: The text requires a disability or long-term condition that affects everyday life, but it does not give the 13-week or 9-month duration conditions.
review.quote: Adult Disability Payment is extra money to help you if you have a disability or long-term health condition that affects your everyday life.

review.name: Carer Support Payment
review.graph: Must provide at least 35 hours of care per week to someone receiving a qualifying disability benefit (ADP, PIP daily living, DLA middle/higher care, AA).
review.note: The 35-hour threshold and the need for the cared-for person to get a qualifying benefit are stated, but the text does not list the qualifying benefits (ADP, PIP daily living, DLA middle/higher care, AA); it only links to a list.

review.name: Carer Support Payment
review.graph: Must live in Scotland.

review.name: Child Disability Payment
review.graph: Child must have a physical or mental disability requiring substantially more care or supervision than a child of the same age, or have difficulty walking.
review.note: The text covers a physical or mental disability needing help, supervision or causing walking difficulty, but never compares the child's needs with those of a child of the same age ('substantially more').
review.quote: It's for a child who, because of their physical or mental disability, either: needs help from another person, for much of the day, to manage their bodily functions

review.name: Child Winter Heating Payment
review.graph: Child must receive the highest rate of the care component of Child Disability Payment (or DLA child).
review.note: The text says the payment is for disabled children and young people, but it never mentions the highest rate of the care component of Child Disability Payment or DLA.
review.quote: It’s a payment to help disabled children and young people and their families with increased heating costs over winter.

review.name: Child Winter Heating Payment
review.graph: Must live in Scotland.

review.name: Funeral Support Payment
review.graph: Must be responsible for arranging or paying for a funeral.

review.name: Funeral Support Payment
review.graph: The funeral must take place in the UK, and applicant must live in Scotland.

review.quote: Funeral Support Payment helps pay for funeral costs if you live in Scotland.

review.name: Workplace Pension auto-enrollment
review.graph: Employing any worker who is aged 22 to State Pension age and earning more than £10,000 per year. Employer obligation — applies from day 1 of taking on qualifying staff.
review.note: The source gives the age range 22 to State Pension age and a £10,000 threshold, and says duties start when the first member of staff starts, but it says "at least £10,000" rather than "more than £10,000" and also requires staff to normally work in the UK, which the criterion leaves out.
review.quote: are aged between 22 and the State Pension age earn at least £10,000 a year

review.name: Check and challenge business rates
review.graph: Must occupy or own a non-domestic property assessed for business rates in England.
review.note: The text covers properties in England or Wales that have a rateable value for business rates and refers to 'your property', but it never says you must occupy or own the property, and it never limits the service to England or to non-domestic property.
review.quote: If you want to report a change to your property or challenge its rateable value, use your business rates valuation account .

review.name: Discretionary Assistance Fund (Wales)
review.graph: EAP: extreme financial hardship or an unexpected crisis with no other money. IAP: must get Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Pension Credit Guarantee Credit or Universal Credit, and be leaving an institution, avoiding going into one, setting up home after an unsettled way of life, moving because of relationship breakdown or domestic abuse, or caring for a released prisoner.
review.note: The text supports extreme financial hardship for the EAP, but it does not mention having no other money, the IAP benefit requirements (Income Support, JSA, ESA, Pension Credit, Universal Credit) or the IAP qualifying situations.
